One Analyst’s Price Target Implies 70% Upside
Netflix has shed more than a third of its value while the broader market climbs, yet one Wall Street analyst sees a path back that would leave today's sellers deeply regretting their exits.
Published September 7, 2026, 8:33am ET · 4 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Netflix currently trades at $78.25 while the average Wall Street price target sits at $93.66. That leaves a gap of roughly 20% between the current quote and consensus.
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) is the world’s largest subscription streaming service, guiding 2026 revenue to $51.0B to $51.4B with an ad-supported tier on track to roughly double. Wall Street has watched the name closely as it flipped from streaming’s untouchable growth story to a battleground stock in the span of nine months. Consensus isn’t even the aggressive read here: BMO Capital Markets carries a Street-high target of $135 on the shares.
What Went Wrong Between January and Summer
Netflix has shed over a third of its value in a year, down 37.77% over 12 months and 16.54% year to date. The unraveling accelerated when Netflix announced an all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. at $27.75 per share in late 2025, pausing buybacks and hitching the story to a $42.2B bridge facility. Q3 2025 earnings then missed on a $619 million Brazilian tax charge that compressed operating margin to 28.2%.
The saga got messier. Netflix terminated the original WBD agreement in Q1 2026 and paid a $2.80B breakup fee, which hit free cash flow through higher cash taxes. Free cash flow fell to $1.53B in Q2 from $2.27B a year earlier. The S&P 500, meanwhile, is up 12.94% year to date. Netflix moved sharply in the opposite direction.
BMO Capital Markets’ Brian Pitz carries the Street-high $135 target, which implies roughly 73% upside from current levels. His Outperform thesis rests on three pillars: an ad-tier monetization super-cycle, a content moat that protects churn and pricing power, and structural margin expansion as advertising and password-sharing revenue flow directly to operating income.
Management has given analysts real numbers to underwrite. Netflix reiterated 13% to 14% full-year revenue growth, roughly $6 billion of incremental revenue, and about $12.5B of free cash flow for 2026. Ad revenue is tracking to ~$3B this year. Q2 buybacks of $4.7B were the largest quarterly repurchase in company history, with $27.1B still authorized.
CFO Spence Neumann framed the runway plainly on the Q2 call: “We’re entertaining an audience approaching a billion people, with still lots of room to grow into our addressable market on every measure.”
Coverage skews bullish. Of the analysts polled, 7 rate the stock Strong Buy, 29 Buy, and 15 Hold, with no active Sells. Recent 30-day revisions have leaned negative as models digest WBD-related noise, but no house has capitulated on the story.
Where Netflix Stands Against Streaming Peers
Netflix fell largely alone. The rest of the streaming complex is a mixed bag.
Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) trades at $105.31 against an average target of $128.18, implying roughly 22% upside. Shares are down 6.71% year to date, cushioned by the Experiences segment. Ratings skew positive with 6 Strong Buy and 24 Buy against 2 Hold and 1 Sell. Real upside, but a fraction of what BMO sees at Netflix.
Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD) trades at $28.25 with an average target of $29.82, or roughly 6% implied upside. WBD is now the subject of a Paramount Skydance merger after Netflix walked, and analyst posture is cautious with 2 Buy, 16 Hold, and 1 Strong Sell. The pending deal caps the story.
Roku (NASDAQ:ROKU) trades at $155.59 versus a $162.33 target, roughly 4% implied upside. Roku is up 43.41% YTD, showing exactly the momentum Netflix lost. Coverage sits at 1 Strong Buy, 9 Buy, 15 Hold, and 1 Strong Sell.
The largest analyst-implied upside in this group sits with Netflix, whether measured against the $93.66 average or BMO’s $135. Peers have re-rated with the market. Netflix has lagged behind that reset.
Netflix trades at $78.25 with an average 12-month target of $93.66 across covering analysts, implying roughly 20% upside, while BMO’s $135 Street-high implies roughly 73%. The stock is down 16.54% year to date and 37.77% over 12 months, against a 12.94% YTD gain and 18.65% one-year return for the S&P 500. Analyst targets are one data point among many.
Forward EPS consensus sits at $3.5844 for 2026 and $3.8184 for 2027, on revenue of $51.22B and $57.01B. Trailing P/E is 25 and forward P/E is 22. Multiples have compressed while the growth trajectory has held.
Netflix looks compelling here if management delivers on the 2026 plan (guided revenue, $12.5B of free cash flow, ~$3B in ad revenue) and if the WBD situation either resolves at reasonable terms or gets abandoned again without further balance sheet damage. The path back to consensus is unglamorous: execute, scale ads, and let the $27.1B remaining buyback authorization keep shrinking the share count.
The bear case rests on the WBD chapter being a strategic mistake priced with real integration and financing risk, or if competitive pressure from Disney, YouTube, and Amazon compresses margins from the current 33.4% operating rate. A $1B debt maturity later in 2026 and ongoing tax disputes add overhang.
My lean: this looks more like a rare value setup for a name that seldom offers one, provided the WBD situation resolves without another surprise. The BMO $135 case requires the entire bull thesis to fire, but even the consensus $93.66 offers a defensible re-rating path from here.

When a stock you own starts trailing the market, it can make you question why you own it. In 2026, anything not deemed an artificial intelligence (AI) "winner" has likely lagged the S&P 500 index. One stand-out laggard is Netflix (NFLX +1.76%).
The streaming mainstay is down around 50% from highs, while the market is up 13% year-to-date (YTD). Should you sell your Netflix stock? Here's why I think its growth opportunity and valuation mean investors should stick with this long-term winning stock.
Image source: Getty Images.

Revenue was up 13% year over year last quarter to $12.6 billion, with stable profit margins. The company no longer reports overall subscriber figures, but it appears the business continues to gain market share in global video streaming. In Asia and Latin America, constant-currency revenue growth exceeded 15%.
Total watch hours grew only 2% year over year in the first half of 2026, but this figure is better than it looks because the World Cup was happening in the second quarter, which Netflix had no rights to. For the long term, Netflix is investing to diversify its content library by adding sports, interactive streaming videos, and live talk shows, including popular podcasts.
By selling this content to a global subscriber base, I believe Netflix is in a much better position than its peers to profit from video streaming. Legacy players like Paramount Skydance or Disney have struggled to gain share in video streaming and have much worse balance sheets than Netflix.
With around half of the United States' watch hours going to streaming today, and even less in some international markets, Netflix should have a sustained demand tailwind to reinvest in while laggards scramble to turn a profit. This is why the company could steadily compound its revenue.
We cannot forget advertising, either, where Netflix is best positioned among all video streamers to grow. Netflix was late to the advertising game, but has recently made a push for cheaper ad-supported subscription tiers to drive more engagement and revenue. It is a small part of the business today, but it should help accelerate revenue growth in the years ahead and give the company more capital to reinvest in areas such as sports rights.
Netflix was in a bidding war for Warner Bros. Studio earlier in 2026. It was planning to buy out the storied production studio for $83 billion before losing in a bidding war to Paramount Skydance. While the deal would have added to its streaming library, investors were unhappy that Netflix entered the bidding war and began selling the stock as a result.
Now, without Warner Bros., Netflix can take its cash and start repurchasing stock at a much lower price. Its outstanding shares have fallen by 6% since beginning its buyback program, which should accelerate given its lower share price. The company used $4.7 billion to repurchase stock in Q2 alone. Apply that over a full year, and Netflix could retire 7% of its outstanding shares at its current market cap of $280 billion.
Right now, Netflix trades at a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 21, which is one of its lowest levels in history. For a business that is growing revenue in the double digits and retiring its outstanding stock, this should lead to solid teen-level earnings per share (EPS) growth in the years ahead. Compared to its P/E ratio, Netflix stock looks very cheap today. Don't sell into this drawdown.

Netflix shares changed hands at EUR 62.78 on the German trading floor, a marginal gain of 0.1% that does little to disguise a bruising month. The gap is stark, and it frames a question that investors are increasingly unwilling to dismiss: can a subscription service justify blockbuster spending when its audience's attention is being siphoned off by free alternatives?
Netflix can still point to genuine scale. Members racked up more than 97 billion viewing hours in the first half of the year — a record for any six-month period. Yet the momentum has a softer edge. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Netflix?
The divergence among analysts is itself telling. Evercore ISI was still calling for higher targets in mid-September, even as the bearish camp gained ground. Management is not standing still. The company is courting high-reach video creators with upfront payments and global licensing deals, hoping to pull talent — and audiences — away from YouTube's ecosystem. Shareholder returns offer some counterweight. In the second quarter alone, Netflix repurchased $4.7 billion worth of its own stock, a signal that management views the recent weakness as a buying opportunity rather than a structural warning.

What are those directors doing from their position for women?” she asks, referencing the men behind other high-profile documentaries this fall, Musk and You Can See Everything. “Until it’s a priority for everyone who says that they care about other people and are interested in a just world, then there won’t be one.
“You’re making a choice for the types of films that you make to look a certain way — you’re making all those choices — and so people will make their choices, and I’ll make mine. My choice is just to try to be self-sustaining,” she continues. “I used to be the poster child of talking about this because I felt like it could make a difference — but what I’ve come to realize is it’s too difficult to do if enough people aren’t on board, and there just aren’t enough people on board. It doesn’t mean give up — it means just do it in other ways.” Her work still continues, for instance, with Array, her sprawling distribution and advocacy company for underrepresented filmmakers.
One way 14th differs from 13th is in the audience DuVernay imagined watching it — particularly its attention span and knowledge base. Early in the process, she ran an informal poll of people at the Grove in Los Angeles, asking what they knew about the Civil War, who fought it and what it was about.
DuVernay with sitting Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden while making 14th.
“The answers were startling, shocking, in terms of people not even having an idea,” she says. “But I don’t want people to feel bad about what they don’t know. I don’t want people to feel overwhelmed.”
The film features historians, current and former senators and members of Congress, and political operatives, but DuVernay widened the mix to include commentators with big online followings, among them Ringer podcaster Van Lathan Jr. and Hasan Piker, the left-wing Twitch flamethrower who has become one of the right’s favorite media bogeymen.
“I would like people to feel like you can enter into this — that this is not going to feel like medicine,” DuVernay says.
Sherrilyn Ifill, former head of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and one of the film’s most prominent legal voices, says DuVernay was unusually good at keeping all that expertise from swallowing the movie.
“I was routinely stunned by how quickly she seemed to absorb detailed information,” she says. “Ava never loses sight of her audience. I had to trust her to bring me back from the minutiae and to remember the ordinary people she hopes to reach with the film.”
As DuVernay puts it, “I wanted different people to be able to see themselves.” Which at times proved to be difficult.
U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel in the Oscar-nominated 2016 doc, which explores the amendment that abolished slavery and its connection to the present-day prison system.
Getting Republicans into the film, for instance, proved a considerable challenge. DuVernay says her team approached nearly 300 GOP officeholders, but only a little more than a dozen engaged with them at all. That group included conservative Trump critics like strategist Steve Schmidt and former Sen. Jeff Flake.
Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna did agree to participate and defends Trump administration policies in the documentary. “Although I am diametrically opposed to almost everything she believes, I had a lot of appreciation for Anna Paulina flying into New York and sitting there with me,” DuVernay says. “No one else would. We asked. I have the receipts.”
DuVernay insists 14th is not a Trump takedown. “He’s a small cog in a wheel that’s been rolling for a very, very long time,” she says. “The current administration is embracing tactics that are tried-and-true and have been tested and weaponized in new ways.”
She thinks of the movie instead as a record — of the history it recounts and the period in which she made it. “COVID, wars, Gaza — it’s been quite a decade, and I don’t think we, as people who experience it, appreciate what we’re living through. They’re going to study this time,” DuVernay says. “My question is, how are we getting our arms around that artistically? This film is like an essay. We were writing through it, about what we discovered, how we felt and what it means.”

Tue, October 6, 2026 at 4:22 PM PDT 4 min read
Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) was trading at around $67 on October 5, down 42.35% over twelve months and close to its 52-week low of $65.08. The company reported net income of $13.65 billion over the past twelve months and free cash flow of $11.15 billion.
Cash arriving behind reported profit is the ordinary shape for a company still building, and it is worth understanding before the share price is.

Is Netflix's (NFLX) Free Cash Flow Keeping Pace With Its Reported Earnings?
The Cash Sits Behind the Profit Because of How Content Is Counted:
The reason sits in how content is counted. Netflix pays for a series up front and then writes the cost off across the years people watch it. The money leaves in one period and the charge against profit lands over several.
That creates a specific signal. When spending on new content runs above the amortization of content already owned, cash falls behind reported profit, because the write-off is still catching up with the paying. Which is exactly the shape of these numbers. On this evidence, the library is being rebuilt rather than harvested.
The underlying business is not the problem. Operating margin is 33.38% and return on equity is 49.54%, on revenue growing 13.40%.

Why the Shares Fell Anyway:
A company generating $11.15 billion of free cash flow has lost 42.35% in a year, so the market is pricing something the cash statement does not show. Start with the growth rates. Revenue grew 13.40%, and earnings grew 8.80%.
Profit rising more slowly than sales says a subscriber business has stopped getting cheaper to run, and for a stock valued on compounding that is the end of the easy part. Now put that beside the cash. Rebuilding a library costs money today and defends subscribers tomorrow, so the spending is the reason the cash gap exists at all.
So the cash gap and the weak share price are not describing the same thing. One is the cost of staying competitive, the other is a judgment on what that spending will buy.
Nothing forces the issue. Debt of $16.65 billion against $9.13 billion of cash is comfortable, and Netflix pays no dividend, so an investor earns nothing while waiting. Earnings growing more slowly than sales is the signal that matters here. Ten stocks positioned for high returns in 2026 are named here.
The Valuation Case:
Sustainability depends on content spending, the one lever management fully controls and the one that trades cash today against subscribers tomorrow. On price, the fall has done a great deal of work, taking the trailing multiple to 22.44 times from 51.08 times a year ago.
Enterprise value to EBITDA of 8.64 is the figure that stands out. For a business earning a 33.38% operating margin, under nine times is what the market pays for companies it expects to be smaller.
Price-to-book of 9.85 is the one measure still carrying a premium. A content library is a decade-long asset or a wasting one depending on what gets spent on it, and we looked at 15 stocks built for the next decade in this list.
Conclusion:
Cash flow is running behind earnings, at $11.15 billion against $13.65 billion, and the reason is that Netflix is paying for new content faster than it writes off the old. At 8.64 times enterprise value to EBITDA on a 33.38% operating margin, the price asks very little. However, earnings grew 8.80% against 13.40% revenue growth, and the spending is not yet buying faster profit. The number to watch is content spending, because it decides whether this gap becomes a catalog or just a cost.

But valuation alone is not sufficient to make an investment decision. How the business is doing is also very important.

The company does have some serious competition, though, including Amazon's Prime Video, Apple's Apple TV, and Alphabet's YouTube. But competition isn't necessarily a deal-breaker. Coca-Cola and PepsiCo have coexisted profitably for decades.

Analyst downgrade puts engagement trends in focus
According to a note from Wells Fargo analyst Steven Cahall dated September 18, 2026, the bank lowered its rating on Netflix from Equal Weight to Underweight and slashed its price target to USD 57 from USD 80, citing weakening viewer engagement trends and concerns about the upcoming content slate.Yahoo Finance The roughly USD 23 reduction in the target represents a cut of about 28.8 percent, and Wells Fargo estimates that the new target implies approximately 20 to 25 percent downside from the level at which Netflix shares had closed before the downgrade.TradingKey
As multiple outlets reported on September 18, 2026, Wells Fargo argued that engagement trends for Netflix’s core streaming service look worrying, with softening viewing intensity per subscriber and expectations for lower margin expansion in 2027 and 2028 as the company prepares less content than previously anticipated for the remainder of 2026.TipRanks In one summary of the downgrade, Wells Fargo warned that Netflix’s share of viewing time could decline and highlighted that its Top 100 originals might face a year-on-year drop in viewing in the second half of 2026, adding to investor concerns about the durability of Netflix’s competitive edge.Inshorts

By September 19, 2026, at least one summary of the recent moves highlighted that Netflix shares had fallen to around USD 70.11, marking the fourth consecutive session of losses and the lowest level in roughly two months.Inshorts The same report noted that the 7 percent decline on that day followed Wells Fargo’s downgrade and that the bank expects Netflix viewership to fall 4 percent year on year in the second half of 2026, including an estimated 20 percent drop for the company’s Top 100 originals, underlining the scale of the engagement risk being priced in.
Despite the negative tone of the downgrade, other recent analysis has pointed to Netflix’s substantial buyback capacity and valuation metrics that some observers describe as offering potential upside. A detailed look at Netflix’s capital allocation published on September 19, 2026 noted that the company repurchased a record USD 4.7 billion of its own shares in the second quarter of 2026 and still had USD 27.1 billion remaining under its existing buyback authorizations at the end of that quarter.Yahoo Finance With Netflix’s market capitalization described in that analysis as roughly USD 326 billion at a share price of about USD 76 as of mid-September 2026, the unused buyback authorization would, in theory, be sufficient to retire about 8 percent of the company’s outstanding shares at that price, a material lever that could support earnings per share over time.
The same buyback-focused commentary emphasized that the record USD 4.7 billion repurchase volume in the second quarter of 2026 significantly exceeded previous quarters, reinforcing that Netflix is actively returning capital to shareholders while continuing to invest in content and its advertising-supported tier.Yahoo Finance For investors, the contrast between Wells Fargo’s caution based on engagement data and the company’s aggressive buyback strategy is an important part of the current debate around Netflix stock, as buybacks can amplify per-share earnings even if topline growth moderates.
Broader analyst consensus remains constructive
While Wells Fargo’s downgrade introduced a rare Sell or Underweight call into the coverage universe, other institutions continue to see upside in Netflix. A September 18, 2026 overview of analyst sentiment noted that Evercore ISI recently raised its price target on Netflix to USD 110, focusing on strong international household penetration, particularly in markets such as the United States and Japan where penetration levels are described as reaching multi-year highs.TradingKey In a separate market wrap dated September 18, 2026, Evercore ISI’s Kutgun Maral was cited as having a USD 110 price target and a positive view based on international growth, underscoring that not all analysts share Wells Fargo’s cautious stance.Yahoo Finance

As of the most recent completed trading day cited in the available data, Netflix stock on Nasdaq had closed at USD 75.31 with the shares later trading intraday around USD 71.72 on September 18, 2026, and reports on September 19, 2026 indicating that the price had dropped to about USD 70.11 at one point, marking a roughly 7 percent daily decline and extending a multi-session losing streak.Inshorts With the stock down about 23 percent year to date as of mid-September 2026 and trading well below bullish price targets in the USD 95 to USD 110 range, but closer to Wells Fargo’s USD 57 downside scenario, investors in Netflix stock now face a sharply polarised analyst landscape that hinges on whether engagement and content trends will weaken or stabilise.

▶ The Challenge of Daily Live Broadcasts for a Month: Netflix and IMG Take on All 64 Matches of the Women's World Cup in Brazil [10/7]
For their first live soccer broadcast, the only thing to rely on in the end is a battle-tested production manual (Image)
Netflix has announced that it has selected IMG, a major sports production company, as its production partner for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, which will be held in Brazil.
The tournament will take place from June 24 to July 25, 2027, and will be the first Women's World Cup held in South America.
Source: [tvtechnology] "Netflix Taps IMG as Production Partner for 2027 Women’s World Cup"
Netflix holds the exclusive streaming rights for the 2027 and 2031 tournaments in the United States and Canada, and this will be the company's first live soccer broadcast.
In addition to broadcasting all 64 matches, IMG will support the production of over 100 hours of studio programming.
Netflix will employ its own unique lineup of play-by-play announcers and commentators.
The broadcasts will be provided in English and Spanish for the U.S., and in English and French for Canada.
Goal! Golazo! But! The shouts in three languages in the Netflix studio (Image)
Prior to the tournament, IMG will also support the live stream of the draw ceremony on December 11, 2026.
IMG is a company with a track record of producing broadcasts for the MLS, the English Football League, and CBS's coverage of the UEFA Champions League.
Netflix positions this tournament as the company's "most ambitious" sports production to date.
Following its ventures into boxing, the NFL, and WWE, this marks a major step forward for the company as it expands its live sports offerings.
What Dinko noted is that Netflix is stepping into the realm of "live every day for about a month."
While the company recorded a peak of 65 million concurrent streams during its boxing broadcast in November 2024, there were a series of reports of streaming issues from before the match through the event itself.
The instantaneous load of a one-off event and the operational load of handling 64 matches day after day are different in nature.
To deliver daily live broadcasts without interruption, both a solid production system and a streaming network that does not fail even when viewership is concentrated are essential.
How much they can learn from the bitter experience of the boxing broadcast will likely be a litmus test for Netflix's future sports streaming.
Their seriousness can also be seen in terms of money.
The broadcast rights fee for the 2027 tournament alone is reported to be approximately $200 million (about 31 billion yen), making it one of the largest contracts for a women's sporting event.
In terms of sports investment by streaming companies, Amazon, which holds the rights to the NBA and NFL, is expected to take the lead, but Netflix has also graduated from the stage of gathering buzz with one-off events and has entered the phase of handling an entire month-long tournament.
Moving forward, they will likely reach out for broadcasting rights to league games throughout the season as well.
With massive rights fees and a full-scale production system in place, it can be said that they have finally entered the main stage of the sports rights battle.
So, in what kind of environment will Japanese viewers welcome the Women's World Cup, which is receiving so much attention across the ocean?
Nadeshiko Japan achieved their third Asian title at the Women's Asian Cup in March 2026 and is ranked 5th in the world in the FIFA rankings announced in June.
They are in a position where they can fully aim for their first world title since 2011.
However, the broadcasting environment remains uncertain.
For the 2023 tournament, domestic television coverage was only decided just one week before the opening, following an agreement between NHK and FIFA.
The 2026 Asian Cup was also exclusively streamed in its entirety by DAZN.
The domestic broadcasting and streaming arrangements for the 2027 tournament do not seem to have been announced yet.
There is a 12-hour time difference with Brazil, and many of Japan's matches will likely be in the early morning or late at night, so a hybrid of 'streaming + terrestrial broadcasting' that combines catch-up streaming, highlights, and documentaries following the players should be the key.
If the tournament, which they are entering as Asian champions, ends up in a situation where people again 'don't know where to watch it,' I think it will be a major loss for the promotion of the sport.
Note that Netflix's rights this time are for the United States and Canada, and do not include streaming the matches in Japan.
However, Netflix has also decided to produce a documentary series related to the tournament, and if such works are streamed in Japan, it could provide a tailwind to increase interest in Nadeshiko.
I felt that the fact that major streaming services have started to invest seriously in women's soccer is a heartening trend.

Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) has retained Wall Street support despite recent concerns over engagement trends, with TD Cowen maintaining its bullish stance on the streaming giant ahead of third-quarter earnings later this month.
The firm reiterated its ‘Buy’ rating and $100 price target on October 5, arguing that Netflix remains positioned for double-digit revenue growth, margin expansion, and higher free cash flow over the coming years.
At Netflix’s current share price of $67.06, the target implies upside of about 49%.
TD Cowen also expects the company’s earnings per share to grow at an annualized rate of roughly 19% between 2026 and 2031, excluding one-time items.
The analyst’s view is based on expectations that Netflix can continue growing revenue while improving profitability through a combination of subscription growth, advertising, and newer content formats.
According to the firm’s latest note, concerns over softer engagement trends have overshadowed several emerging growth drivers.
TD Cowen highlighted live content, podcasts, vertical video initiatives, and the company’s advertising-supported tier as areas that could boost engagement while supporting subscriber growth and retention.
While the firm modestly lowered some operating income and EBITDA estimates for the coming years, it maintained its $100 valuation target after rolling its discounted cash flow model forward to 2027.
The analyst also pointed to Netflix’s relatively modest valuation compared to its long-term growth outlook. Based on TD Cowen’s estimates, the stock trades at about 17 times projected 2027 earnings, while the $100 target implies a multiple of roughly 25 times expected earnings.
TD Cowen’s latest call broadly aligns with Wall Street sentiment. Analyst consensus data currently at TradingView rates Netflix a ‘Buy’, with the average 12-month price target standing at approximately $92.53. The highest target on the stock is $135, while the lowest forecast is $57.
Netflix stock 12-month prediction. Source: TradingView
Investors are now focused on Netflix’s third-quarter earnings report scheduled for October 20. Wall Street expects the company to post earnings of about $0.82 per share on revenue of roughly $12.87 billion to $12.88 billion, representing year-over-year revenue growth of nearly 12%.
Those estimates are broadly in line with Netflix’s own guidance issued alongside second-quarter results, when the company projected third-quarter revenue of $12.86 billion and earnings per share of $0.82.

Are Rising Live Sports Costs a Margin Threat to Netflix Stockholders?
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 7:12 AM PDT 3 min read
Netflix's NFLX expanding live sports slate is turning into a cost line investors can no longer treat as experimental. In September, the streamer kicked off its NFL schedule with the league's first regular-season game in Australia, part of an extension through the 2029-30 season covering a Week 1 game, a Thanksgiving Eve matchup, Christmas Day, a Week 18 finale and the NFL Honors. Netflix also confirmed that Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will fight live on Dec. 11, while 2027 brings exclusive U.S. and Canada rights to the FIFA Women's World Cup.
The economics are lopsided. Netflix expects live programming to absorb just over 5% of 2026 content spend while generating only about 1% of view hours. Its defense rests on acquisition: live events accounted for six of the 10 biggest new-member sign-up days over the past five years. Yet that payoff is episodic, while rights costs recur.
Cash outlays are rising faster than earnings. Additions to content assets jumped 32% year over year to $9.8 billion in the first half of 2026, outpacing the 11% rise in content amortization, while capital expenditure climbed 46% to $415 million. Second-quarter operating margin contracted 70 basis points to 33.4%, and free cash flow fell to $1.5 billion from $2.3 billion, partly due to higher cash taxes.
Guidance offers partial comfort. Netflix narrowed 2026 revenues to $51.0-$51.4 billion and maintained a 31.5% operating margin target versus 29.5% in 2025, with ad revenues expected to double to about $3 billion. Third-quarter margin is projected at 33.2%.
However, the full-year target implies a fourth-quarter margin near 27%, in a quarter loaded with NFL holiday games and the Fury-Joshua bout. With content obligations at $25.1 billion and a cash content-to-amortization ratio of about 1.1x, sports escalation could test margin expansion beyond 2026.
How Disney and Amazon Are Managing Live Sports Costs
Disney DIS offers a direct read on sports cost inflation. In third-quarter fiscal 2026, Disney's Sports segment operating income fell 17% to $858 million, as programming and production costs rose 10% to $3.05 billion despite 4% revenue growth. Disney is pushing more ESPN games onto Disney+ this fall to broaden reach. Amazon AMZN presents a monetization-led contrast. Amazon's advertising revenues grew 26% year over year to $19.8 billion in the second quarter of 2026, with Thursday Night Football, NBA, WNBA and NASCAR inventory selling out. However, Amazon does not separately disclose the profitability of its Prime Video sports rights.
NFLX's Price Performance, Valuation & Estimates
Netflix's shares have plunged 28% year to date, underperforming the Zacks Broadcast Radio and Television industry and Zacks Consumer Discretionary sector's decline of 20.1% and 14.7%, respectively.
Netflix's valuation remains elevated, with the stock trading at a forward 12-month price/sales ratio of 5.04X versus the industry's 3.52X. NFLX carries a Value Score of D.
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NFLX's 2026 earnings is pegged at $3.59 per share and remains unchanged over the past 30 days. This indicates a 41.9% increase from the previous year.

Netflix Has Momentum Despite Being Down in 2026. One Analyst’s Price Target Implies 70% Upside
Netflix has shed more than a third of its value while the broader market climbs, yet one Wall Street analyst sees a path back that would leave today's sellers deeply regretting their exits.
Published September 7, 2026, 8:33am ET · 4 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Netflix currently trades at $78.25 while the average Wall Street price target sits at $93.66. That leaves a gap of roughly 20% between the current quote and consensus.
Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX | NFLX Price Prediction) is the world’s largest subscription streaming service, guiding 2026 revenue to $51.0B to $51.4B with an ad-supported tier on track to roughly double. Wall Street has watched the name closely as it flipped from streaming’s untouchable growth story to a battleground stock in the span of nine months. Consensus isn’t even the aggressive read here: BMO Capital Markets carries a Street-high target of $135 on the shares.
What Went Wrong Between January and Summer
Netflix has shed over a third of its value in a year, down 37.77% over 12 months and 16.54% year to date. The unraveling accelerated when Netflix announced an all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. at $27.75 per share in late 2025, pausing buybacks and hitching the story to a $42.2B bridge facility. Q3 2025 earnings then missed on a $619 million Brazilian tax charge that compressed operating margin to 28.2%.
The saga got messier. Netflix terminated the original WBD agreement in Q1 2026 and paid a $2.80B breakup fee, which hit free cash flow through higher cash taxes. Free cash flow fell to $1.53B in Q2 from $2.27B a year earlier. The S&P 500, meanwhile, is up 12.94% year to date. Netflix moved sharply in the opposite direction.
BMO Capital Markets’ Brian Pitz carries the Street-high $135 target, which implies roughly 73% upside from current levels. His Outperform thesis rests on three pillars: an ad-tier monetization super-cycle, a content moat that protects churn and pricing power, and structural margin expansion as advertising and password-sharing revenue flow directly to operating income.
Management has given analysts real numbers to underwrite. Netflix reiterated 13% to 14% full-year revenue growth, roughly $6 billion of incremental revenue, and about $12.5B of free cash flow for 2026. Ad revenue is tracking to ~$3B this year. Q2 buybacks of $4.7B were the largest quarterly repurchase in company history, with $27.1B still authorized.
CFO Spence Neumann framed the runway plainly on the Q2 call: “We’re entertaining an audience approaching a billion people, with still lots of room to grow into our addressable market on every measure.”
Coverage skews bullish. Of the analysts polled, 7 rate the stock Strong Buy, 29 Buy, and 15 Hold, with no active Sells. Recent 30-day revisions have leaned negative as models digest WBD-related noise, but no house has capitulated on the story.
Where Netflix Stands Against Streaming Peers
Netflix fell largely alone. The rest of the streaming complex is a mixed bag.
Walt Disney (NYSE:DIS) trades at $105.31 against an average target of $128.18, implying roughly 22% upside. Shares are down 6.71% year to date, cushioned by the Experiences segment. Ratings skew positive with 6 Strong Buy and 24 Buy against 2 Hold and 1 Sell. Real upside, but a fraction of what BMO sees at Netflix.
Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD) trades at $28.25 with an average target of $29.82, or roughly 6% implied upside. WBD is now the subject of a Paramount Skydance merger after Netflix walked, and analyst posture is cautious with 2 Buy, 16 Hold, and 1 Strong Sell. The pending deal caps the story.
Roku (NASDAQ:ROKU) trades at $155.59 versus a $162.33 target, roughly 4% implied upside. Roku is up 43.41% YTD, showing exactly the momentum Netflix lost. Coverage sits at 1 Strong Buy, 9 Buy, 15 Hold, and 1 Strong Sell.
The largest analyst-implied upside in this group sits with Netflix, whether measured against the $93.66 average or BMO’s $135. Peers have re-rated with the market. Netflix has lagged behind that reset.
Netflix trades at $78.25 with an average 12-month target of $93.66 across covering analysts, implying roughly 20% upside, while BMO’s $135 Street-high implies roughly 73%. The stock is down 16.54% year to date and 37.77% over 12 months, against a 12.94% YTD gain and 18.65% one-year return for the S&P 500. Analyst targets are one data point among many.
Forward EPS consensus sits at $3.5844 for 2026 and $3.8184 for 2027, on revenue of $51.22B and $57.01B. Trailing P/E is 25 and forward P/E is 22. Multiples have compressed while the growth trajectory has held.
Netflix looks compelling here if management delivers on the 2026 plan (guided revenue, $12.5B of free cash flow, ~$3B in ad revenue) and if the WBD situation either resolves at reasonable terms or gets abandoned again without further balance sheet damage. The path back to consensus is unglamorous: execute, scale ads, and let the $27.1B remaining buyback authorization keep shrinking the share count.
The bear case rests on the WBD chapter being a strategic mistake priced with real integration and financing risk, or if competitive pressure from Disney, YouTube, and Amazon compresses margins from the current 33.4% operating rate. A $1B debt maturity later in 2026 and ongoing tax disputes add overhang.
My lean: this looks more like a rare value setup for a name that seldom offers one, provided the WBD situation resolves without another surprise. The BMO $135 case requires the entire bull thesis to fire, but even the consensus $93.66 offers a defensible re-rating path from here.

When a stock you own starts trailing the market, it can make you question why you own it. In 2026, anything not deemed an artificial intelligence (AI) "winner" has likely lagged the S&P 500 index. One stand-out laggard is Netflix (NFLX +1.76%).
The streaming mainstay is down around 50% from highs, while the market is up 13% year-to-date (YTD). Should you sell your Netflix stock? Here's why I think its growth opportunity and valuation mean investors should stick with this long-term winning stock.
Image source: Getty Images.
Netflix has a narrative that the company is ripe for disruption by social platforms like Alphabet's YouTube and AI-generated content. So far, this has not impacted its financial performance.
$281BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Revenue was up 13% year over year last quarter to $12.6 billion, with stable profit margins. The company no longer reports overall subscriber figures, but it appears the business continues to gain market share in global video streaming. In Asia and Latin America, constant-currency revenue growth exceeded 15%.
Total watch hours grew only 2% year over year in the first half of 2026, but this figure is better than it looks because the World Cup was happening in the second quarter, which Netflix had no rights to. For the long term, Netflix is investing to diversify its content library by adding sports, interactive streaming videos, and live talk shows, including popular podcasts.
By selling this content to a global subscriber base, I believe Netflix is in a much better position than its peers to profit from video streaming. Legacy players like Paramount Skydance or Disney have struggled to gain share in video streaming and have much worse balance sheets than Netflix.
With around half of the United States' watch hours going to streaming today, and even less in some international markets, Netflix should have a sustained demand tailwind to reinvest in while laggards scramble to turn a profit. This is why the company could steadily compound its revenue.
We cannot forget advertising, either, where Netflix is best positioned among all video streamers to grow. Netflix was late to the advertising game, but has recently made a push for cheaper ad-supported subscription tiers to drive more engagement and revenue. It is a small part of the business today, but it should help accelerate revenue growth in the years ahead and give the company more capital to reinvest in areas such as sports rights.
Netflix was in a bidding war for Warner Bros. Studio earlier in 2026. It was planning to buy out the storied production studio for $83 billion before losing in a bidding war to Paramount Skydance. While the deal would have added to its streaming library, investors were unhappy that Netflix entered the bidding war and began selling the stock as a result.
Now, without Warner Bros., Netflix can take its cash and start repurchasing stock at a much lower price. Its outstanding shares have fallen by 6% since beginning its buyback program, which should accelerate given its lower share price. The company used $4.7 billion to repurchase stock in Q2 alone. Apply that over a full year, and Netflix could retire 7% of its outstanding shares at its current market cap of $280 billion.
Right now, Netflix trades at a price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) of 21, which is one of its lowest levels in history. For a business that is growing revenue in the double digits and retiring its outstanding stock, this should lead to solid teen-level earnings per share (EPS) growth in the years ahead. Compared to its P/E ratio, Netflix stock looks very cheap today. Don't sell into this drawdown.

Netflix shares changed hands at EUR 62.78 on the German trading floor, a marginal gain of 0.1% that does little to disguise a bruising month. Over the past 30 days, the stock has shed 11% — a retreat that coincides with a broader reassessment of whether paid streaming's growth engine can keep humming in a landscape where free, user-generated video is eating into viewing time.
The anxiety crystallized this week when HSBC downgraded Netflix from "Buy" to "Hold," slashing its price target from $96 to $76. Analyst Mohammed Khallouf pointed to a thin pipeline of genuine crowd-pullers and flagged YouTube as an increasingly formidable rival — not the traditional Hollywood studios, but a platform that operates on an entirely different economic model. Days earlier, on September 18, Wells Fargo's Steven Cahall had gone further, cutting his target from $80 to $57 and slapping an "Underweight" rating on the stock.
Nielsen data for July lays bare the scale of the shift. YouTube captured 14.2% of all US television viewing that month, while Netflix managed 7.8%. The gap is stark, and it frames a question that investors are increasingly unwilling to dismiss: can a subscription service justify blockbuster spending when its audience's attention is being siphoned off by free alternatives?
Netflix can still point to genuine scale. Members racked up more than 97 billion viewing hours in the first half of the year — a record for any six-month period. Yet the momentum has a softer edge. Viewing hours for English-language top-10 titles fell roughly 17% year-on-year across July and August, a decline that gave HSBC and Wells Fargo the ammunition for their more cautious stances.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Netflix?
The divergence among analysts is itself telling. Evercore ISI was still calling for higher targets in mid-September, even as the bearish camp gained ground. Such a wide spread of opinion suggests the market has entered a genuine period of reorientation, with no consensus on where Netflix's fair value lies.
Betting on Ads, Creators, and Live Sports
Management is not standing still. The company is courting high-reach video creators with upfront payments and global licensing deals, hoping to pull talent — and audiences — away from YouTube's ecosystem. YouTube, for its part, unveiled new tools for short-form content, automated dubbing, and editing assistance, tightening its grip on creators and protecting its advertising revenue.
On the monetization front, Netflix is leaning harder into advertising and selective price increases. For full-year 2026, the company is targeting roughly $3 billion in ad revenue — a figure that would double the prior year's tally. The advertiser base already exceeded 4,000 at the start of the year. In the UK, subscription prices have been raised, with the ad-supported entry tier now costing GBP 7.99 per month.
Live programming is another lever. Netflix is expanding its sports slate, adding NFL games to a growing roster of real-time events designed to draw viewers who might otherwise drift to free platforms.
Shareholder returns offer some counterweight. In the second quarter alone, Netflix repurchased $4.7 billion worth of its own stock, a signal that management views the recent weakness as a buying opportunity rather than a structural warning.
The real verdict, however, comes on October 20, when Netflix reports third-quarter 2026 results. By then, the market will want more than reassurances. Investors are demanding operational discipline and consistent monetization — not the promise of subscriber records that once justified any valuation. If the autumn numbers confirm that viewers are permanently shifting their hours toward alternative video formats, margin pressure will intensify. Streaming has grown up, and with maturity comes a colder calculus of costs and returns.

Netflix (NFLX) Stock Drops After CEO Admits Slower Growth
Netflix (NFLX) stock fell 1% as analysts split on its outlook and Co-CEO Sarandos admitted growth has slowed ahead of Q3 earnings.
By Trader EdgeOctober 1, 20264 Mins Read
Netflix stock dropped 1% on Wednesday, trading as low as $69.51 before settling at $69.58.
The stock sits below both its 50-day ($75.79) and 200-day ($82.73) moving averages.
Analysts are split: Deutsche Bank and Evercore ISI raised targets, while HSBC and Wells Fargo downgraded the stock.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted growth is slower than he wants, though he says the business is “growing fine.”
Third-quarter earnings will be the next big test, with investors watching subscriber numbers, pricing, and ad revenue.
Netflix (NFLX) stock fell 1% during Wednesday trading, dipping to $69.51 before closing the session at $69.58. Trading volume came in at roughly 34.5 million shares, well below the average of 42.6 million.
The drop pushes Netflix further under its key technical levels. Its 50-day moving average sits at $75.79, and its 200-day average is $82.73, meaning the stock remains well off its recent highs.
Despite the slide, Wall Street opinion on Netflix is far from united. Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to Buy from Hold this week, pointing to international engagement growth and the company’s use of AI in production and advertising.
Evercore ISI also raised its price target to $110, keeping an Outperform rating. The firm highlighted stronger market penetration in the U.S. and Japan, plus upcoming live programming like Netflix’s exclusive Japanese WWE rights starting October 1.
Not everyone is convinced. HSBC downgraded Netflix to Hold, citing competition from YouTube and a still-small advertising contribution to overall revenue.
Wells Fargo went further, cutting its rating to Underweight with a $57 price target. The firm pointed to concerns that Netflix’s growth is maturing faster than new revenue streams can replace it.
The result is a consensus rating of Moderate Buy, with an average price target of $95.15. That is a wide gap from where the stock trades today.
Rising content spending adds another wrinkle. Netflix continues to commit heavily to new productions, and that upfront spending could squeeze free cash flow even as revenue keeps climbing.
On the earnings side, Netflix beat expectations in its last report. The company posted $0.80 in earnings per share against a $0.79 estimate, with revenue of $12.56 billion, up 13.4% year over year.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos spoke directly to the slowdown at the Bloomberg Screentime conference this week. “Overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster,” he said.
Sarandos pointed to live programming as part of the strategy. Live content makes up about 5% of Netflix’s $20 billion annual content budget but drives a disproportionate number of new signups.
He also walked back his comment slightly, adding that “the business is great and growing fine.” When asked about Netflix’s past pursuit of Warner Bros. Discovery, Sarandos simply replied, “Nahhh.”
On the subject of streaming market share following the Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance consolidation, Sarandos said it’s too early to know how things will shake out. “It looks on paper, so far it’s one and one,” he said.
Insider activity has also drawn attention. CFO Spencer Neumann sold over 9,000 shares in August, while insiders overall have sold more than 179,000 shares worth over $13 million in the past ninety days.
Institutional investors still hold the majority of the stock, with ownership at roughly 81%. Several firms added to their positions during the first quarter, even as the share price has slipped since.
Looking ahead, third-quarter earnings will be the next real catalyst. Investors will be watching subscriber trends, ad revenue growth, and management’s commentary on cash flow heading into the new year.

Josh Hartnett and Mackenzie Davis, Below
The trailer for Netflix's Below understandably paints it as a thriller about a marine monster terrorizing a coastal town, but there's a lot more to Below if you go deeper. Yes, there's something monstrous in the water, and that's the bait that will bring viewers in, but Below wants to be more than just seaside scares.
Created by Jesse McKeown, the co-showrunner for The Umbrella Academy and a writer on Letterkenny and The Sinner, Below mixes horror, drama, and even comedy as it follows Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett), a fisherman in Newfoundland, Canada, and Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis), a marine zoologist, as they fight to protect the community against the mysterious beast.
"The way that it was sort of described to me is that there's a hook in this show," Hartnett told TV Guide. "It's set in Newfoundland, and there's something about it that everybody's going to respond to, but that's not really what the show is about. It's mostly about what happens underneath the surface. I know that sounds like another tagline, but it is true in many different senses."
Everything you need for fall TV:
The most anticipated shows coming this fall
The ultimate guide to what to watch in October
Calvin's young adult children, Jay (Rohan Campbell), Mary (Ruby Stokes), and Wade (Charlie Heaton), each present their own challenges for Calvin. Jay and Mary are visiting from the mainland after spreading their wings and escaping the remote fishing island, while island-bound Wade wishes to prove himself to everyone, including his dad, with whom he runs an Airbnb out of their small home to rugged and eager tourists. But everyone is in the midst of change, whether it's sought out or forced upon them.
"It's a show that's about family, but a show that's about something supernatural, and it's a show that's about our times and what we've lost, and what we could regain," Hartnett added. "And I think it's a beautifully written show, and I loved the experience of making it."
"It is on paper really, really hard to describe," Heaton said.
That theme of change propels Below. Climate change is affecting the sealife and reshaping the coasts, the young Penneys are in the adulting transition from dependence to independence, and even the town itself is on the verge of packing itself up and joining the rest of Canada.
Filmed on location in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada's easternmost province, Below will take many to a world they've never experienced before, certainly on television, where only a handful of shows (the Canadians series Son of a Critch, Saint-Pierre, and Hudson & Rex, for example) have been set. McKeown's wife is from Newfoundland, so he was instantly drawn to making a TV show upon visiting there. With its gorgeous coasts, isolated towns, and strong Irish-Canadian roots (which create one of North America's most distinctive accents; just wait until you hear Heaton's interpretation of it), Newfoundland plays a major part in the show. And its history of government-forced resettlement programs, during which homes were literally floated across the ocean to the mainland, is intertwined with the story.
"What appealed to me and I think all of us is — this like is the difficult thing to describe — which is that it's an extremely site-specific story about a community that hasn't been represented a lot," Davis, a native of Vancouver, B.C., told TV Guide. "That like I have a lot of curiosity about. I'm sure the rest of the world — Canada knows very little about [Newfoundland] let alone the rest of the world. [It's] an incredibly artistic, funny, creative community of fishermen and people and folklore." She continued, "And coming from Vancouver, it's on the other side of the world from me. I mean, Canada's enormous. I'd never been there. I never knew if I would go there, and to actually get to plant my feet in the soil was such a gift."
Because it's a six-episode limited series, Below doesn't have lots of time to spend in Newfoundland, or with the family drama of the Penneys, or in the boisterous bars with the locals where tourists are required to kiss a dead fish when they order a drink. But you'll likely wish you could spend more time there as the horror and drama mix together in this indescribable show that straddles genres.
And as Davis adds, "On top of that, it's funny. Like what the f**k?"

Netflix has given a pilot order to “Angus, Thongs and Full-Frontal Snogging,” a series adaptation of Louise Rennison’s young adult novels. Fifth Season and Rise Films are producing the project.
If greenlit, the Netflix series will mark the second screen adaptation of Rennison’s books. Netflix declined to comment on the pilot order.
Both the books and the 2008 film follow a British teenager named Georgia. Netflix has added My Hero Academia: Vigilantes to its library in many regions today, October 6th, with both seasons of the spin-off now available to stream. The US isn’t alone, either, as the series has also arrived in most other Netflix regions, including the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.
Netflix has been steadily building out its My Hero Academia catalog over the past year. We’ve recently covered the arrival of the missing seasons of the main series, the multi-country release of My Hero Academia: You’re Next, and the live-action adaptation in the works (maybe, hopefully still?). Vigilantes is the latest piece of the franchise to land.
Here’s what you need to know about the new addition, where it’s streaming, and how the franchise has performed on Netflix so far.
What is My Hero Academia: Vigilantes?
Set before the events of the main series, Vigilantes follows Koichi Haimawari (voiced by Shuichiro Umeda), a timid college student whose dreams of becoming a pro hero never panned out. After a life-changing incident, he accepts an offer from the hulking vigilante Knuckleduster (Yasuhiro Mamiya) to train as his protégé. Alongside the pop-idol vigilante PopStep (Ikumi Hasegawa), they take on the street-level crimes that licensed pro heroes overlook.
Both seasons are now streaming, totaling 26 episodes (13 per season [VERIFY]). The series is available in Japanese with [English subtitles / English dub — VERIFY] on Netflix.
Where is Vigilantes streaming on Netflix?
As of today, Vigilantes is streaming in the US and most other Netflix regions, including (but not limited to):
The series premiered on Crunchyroll in April 2025, which is why it hadn’t been on Netflix in these regions until now.
However, Netflix subscribers in parts of Asia have been able to watch Vigilantes for some time. Netflix previously licensed the series across several Asian territories in 2025:
Japan, Hong Kong, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand: October 17, 2025
How popular is My Hero Academia on Netflix?
Netflix’s bi-annual engagement reports, covering January 2023 through June 2026, show My Hero Academia has been one of the streamer’s most consistent anime performers. Across 14 seasons and movies, the franchise has racked up 728.5 million hours viewed and just over 100 million views, and that’s despite regional differences in availability.
Season 1 has drawn the most views of any entry at 18.1 million, while Season 2 leads in watch time with 151.6 million hours. The Vigilantes figures so far come only from the Asian territories where it was previously available, so expect a significant jump once the US, UK and other major regions are factored into the next report.
Figures cover January 2023 to June 2026, or from when each title first appeared in the reports.
Will there be a Season 3 of Vigilantes?
A third season of My Hero Academia: Vigilantes hasn’t been confirmed yet. Season 1 aired in spring 2025 and Season 2 followed in winter 2026, but no renewal was announced after the Season 2 finale. Studio Bones is currently busy with other franchise projects, including the 10th anniversary short My Hero Academia: I Am a Hero Too. There’s still plenty of manga left to adapt, however, so a return is far from ruled out.
If a third season is confirmed, we’ll keep you posted on whether it’s heading to Netflix.
Will you be checking out My Hero Academia: Vigilantes on Netflix? Let us know in the comments below!

pages.text:
Ava DuVernay in 2023.
Gioncarlo Valentine/The New York Times/Redux
In an early September morning over breakfast on a restaurant patio in her Eastside L.A. neighborhood, Ava DuVernay is remembering a piece of advice Steven Spielberg gave her more than a decade ago.
Around the release of Selma, the fiery 2014 historical drama that received a best picture Oscar nomination, DuVernay attended a dinner at J.J. Abrams’ house and found herself seated next to Spielberg. Her movie was launching her into a new sphere of opportunity — and visibility — in Hollywood, and there, a few inches away, was arguably the most famous filmmaker in the world. She marveled to Spielberg, “Your name is on so many things — even things that you don’t direct,” before asking how he handled the pressure of delivering every time. What if a project left his fans or peers disappointed?
Jamie Foxx Does Not Want to Be Canceled Over New Hulu Stand-up Special: "After That Kevin Hart Roast, I Had to Cut Everything"
Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters
“He said, ‘You make another one,’ ” DuVernay recalls. ” ‘You just keep going.’ “
DuVernay has held that advice close ever since. This morning, she’s only a few weeks from the New York Film Festival premiere of her latest film, 14th, a documentary about the 14th Amendment and its increasingly fraught place in American political life. It’s a companion piece to her Oscar-nominated 2016 documentary 13th, which examined mass incarceration and the prison-industrial complex through the amendment that abolished slavery.
The new film also comes on the heels of Origin, DuVernay’s ambitious 2023 narrative drama, which resonated with critics but — like even a few Spielberg movies — underperformed with audiences. “I’ve talked to a lot of fellow filmmakers about that experience,” she says. “Some really famous, well-known guy friends reminded me that everyone has films that are not as widely seen as they should be.”
And so, on to the next.
The director on the set of her 2023 narrative drama Origin.
The idea for 14th came to DuVernay in early 2024, when Donald Trump, campaigning to return to the White House, was promising to challenge birthright citizenship — one of the rights enshrined in the 14th Amendment. At first, that gave her the movie’s frame. Then the frame kept widening.
Once Trump was back in office, the amendment seemed to keep turning up in the news: due process, public debt, even its language around “insurrection or rebellion.” What had begun as a film about one contested constitutional guarantee was becoming something larger — and, for DuVernay, harder to pin down while history was still moving beneath her feet.
“This movie kicked my butt because it was like building a plane midflight — so much stuff was coming in every day, everything was happening,” DuVernay says.
During production, she followed Carla Hayden, the first African American and first woman to serve as librarian of Congress; three weeks later, Hayden was fired. She followed Dr. Lonnie Bunch, the first Black secretary of the Smithsonian Institution who later retired amid speculation of political pressure, which Bunch has denied.
“All my feelings about everything happening in the past three years — creatively, politically, socially, culturally — are being put into this film,” she says. “At least I’ve felt productive and not like I was going crazy with worry and fear and anger.”
For 14th, DuVernay interviewed more than 50 experts, scholars and politicians, interweaving their insights with vérité interludes and brief snippets of relevant stand-up from comedians like Hasan Minhaj. “Comedians are the last frontier of truth-telling,” she says.
The film was made for Netflix, which DuVernay considers her “home studio,” having worked with the Ted Sarandos- and Greg Peters-run streamer on such projects as 13th. But 14th arrives as some of Hollywood’s largest companies have come under scrutiny for their handling of politically sensitive material. Amazon dropped the Sam Altman docudrama Artificial with the statement, “We believe that Artificial will be better served if it were released by a different studio,” after striking a major deal with Altman’s OpenAI. (Neon quickly picked it up.) Apple, meanwhile, pushed the Jessica Chastain political-violence thriller The Savant by more than a year after the assassination of Charlie Kirk; Chastain later said she was “not aligned” with that decision.
DuVernay interviews activist and philosopher Angela Davis for 13th.
14th ranks among the more overtly political projects Netflix has backed, and DuVernay wondered whether the company would stay out of her way. “I was really hopeful that they would continue to support the filmmakers in the way that they’ve established — and they did,” she says. “I was hoping they would hold their stance under what has felt like a lot of pressure to do otherwise. … In this climate, I would’ve expected a little more ‘helicopter mom.’ ”
The cancellation of Stephen Colbert’s late night show, the turmoil around Jimmy Kimmel and Paramount’s settlement of Trump’s lawsuit against 60 Minutes all registered with DuVernay as she worked. Most unnerving was the short-lived merger agreement between Warner Bros. Discovery and Netflix, which drew attention in Washington.
“I was like, ‘What’s this merger? What’s happening? What’s going on?’ ” DuVernay recalls asking Adam Del Deo, Netflix’s vp docs. “He said, ‘Ava, just keep making the movie you want to make. I can’t tell you what’s going to happen. I really don’t know what’s happening.’ “
She then asked, “Are you guys going to drop this?”
Del Deo responded, “I don’t know. Just keep making it.”
“I feel like everyone’s afraid, and I’m no exception — I’ve been cautioned about this material and about my points of view on all kinds of things,” DuVernay says. “We’ve seen a total recession in films by certain kinds of people and movies made for certain amounts of money — I think artists and executives feel a lot less free.”
A former film publicist, DuVernay broke out behind the camera in the 2010s with the emotional, character-driven indies I Will Follow and Middle of Nowhere. Since then, she has moved across documentaries, limited series and big studio movies. Her 2018 Disney tentpole A Wrinkle in Time disappointed at the box office; a year later came the massively popular and Emmy-winning When They See Us.
Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor stars in the film, based on Isabel Wilkerson’s Caste: The Origins of Our Discontents.
Over time, she has grown less interested in being one of the industry’s designated spokespeople on representation. “Is Alex Gibney going to get that question? Is Nathan Fielder going to get that question? What are those directors doing from their position for women?” she asks, referencing the men behind other high-profile documentaries this fall, Musk and You Can See Everything. “Until it’s a priority for everyone who says that they care about other people and are interested in a just world, then there won’t be one.
“You’re making a choice for the types of films that you make to look a certain way — you’re making all those choices — and so people will make their choices, and I’ll make mine. My choice is just to try to be self-sustaining,” she continues. “I used to be the poster child of talking about this because I felt like it could make a difference — but what I’ve come to realize is it’s too difficult to do if enough people aren’t on board, and there just aren’t enough people on board. It doesn’t mean give up — it means just do it in other ways.” Her work still continues, for instance, with Array, her sprawling distribution and advocacy company for underrepresented filmmakers.
One way 14th differs from 13th is in the audience DuVernay imagined watching it — particularly its attention span and knowledge base. Early in the process, she ran an informal poll of people at the Grove in Los Angeles, asking what they knew about the Civil War, who fought it and what it was about.
DuVernay with sitting Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden while making 14th.
“The answers were startling, shocking, in terms of people not even having an idea,” she says. “But I don’t want people to feel bad about what they don’t know. I don’t want people to feel overwhelmed.”
The film features historians, current and former senators and members of Congress, and political operatives, but DuVernay widened the mix to include commentators with big online followings, among them Ringer podcaster Van Lathan Jr. and Hasan Piker, the left-wing Twitch flamethrower who has become one of the right’s favorite media bogeymen.
“I would like people to feel like you can enter into this — that this is not going to feel like medicine,” DuVernay says.
Sherrilyn Ifill, former head of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and one of the film’s most prominent legal voices, says DuVernay was unusually good at keeping all that expertise from swallowing the movie.
“I was routinely stunned by how quickly she seemed to absorb detailed information,” she says. “Ava never loses sight of her audience. I had to trust her to bring me back from the minutiae and to remember the ordinary people she hopes to reach with the film.”
As DuVernay puts it, “I wanted different people to be able to see themselves.” Which at times proved to be difficult.
U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel in the Oscar-nominated 2016 doc, which explores the amendment that abolished slavery and its connection to the present-day prison system.
Getting Republicans into the film, for instance, proved a considerable challenge. DuVernay says her team approached nearly 300 GOP officeholders, but only a little more than a dozen engaged with them at all. That group included conservative Trump critics like strategist Steve Schmidt and former Sen. Jeff Flake.
Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna did agree to participate and defends Trump administration policies in the documentary. “Although I am diametrically opposed to almost everything she believes, I had a lot of appreciation for Anna Paulina flying into New York and sitting there with me,” DuVernay says. “No one else would. We asked. I have the receipts.”
DuVernay insists 14th is not a Trump takedown. “He’s a small cog in a wheel that’s been rolling for a very, very long time,” she says. “The current administration is embracing tactics that are tried-and-true and have been tested and weaponized in new ways.”
She thinks of the movie instead as a record — of the history it recounts and the period in which she made it. “COVID, wars, Gaza — it’s been quite a decade, and I don’t think we, as people who experience it, appreciate what we’re living through. They’re going to study this time,” DuVernay says. “My question is, how are we getting our arms around that artistically? This film is like an essay. We were writing through it, about what we discovered, how we felt and what it means.”

Netflix has now officially greenlighted the drama series Feral, setting three for lead roles opposite Baby Reindeer‘s Jessica Gunning: Michelle Dockery (Downton Abbey), Genevieve O’Reilly (Andor) and Quintessa Swindell (Prime Target).
The show, from creator Jude Mack, has also newly cast Dolly de Leon (Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed).
Dockery will play Julia, with O’Reilly as Silvana, Swindless as Suzy, and De Leon as Elena. We announced Gunning’s casting as Annie in September. Production is due to begin in Australia this year.

Based on the 1987 novel Savages by Shirley Conran, Feral follows four very different women who accompany their mining executive husbands on a corporate holiday to a beautiful but lethal tropical island. When the men’s shady deals land them all in danger, the women must learn to survive the jungle — and each other. The question is, can they put aside their differences, self-doubts and vanities to stay alive?
Mack wrote the seven-episode series and exec produces alongside its director, Emma Freeman, as well as Liza Marshall and Bria Thomas for Hera Pictures, Hamish Lewis and David Belshaw for Warner Bros. International Television Production. Laurie Borg is series producer.
Billing Feral as “a wild, messy journey of self-discovery,” Mack said, “It’s a complete dream to be carrying Shirley Conran’s torch alongside Hera and Netflix. I can’t wait for people to meet these funny, brutal, bold women. I’m obsessed with them and hope audiences will be too.”
Hera Pictures’ founder, Marshall, added: “We’re delighted to be working with the incredibly talented Jude Mack to bring Shirley Conran’s best-selling novel to the screen. The extraordinary female characters at the heart of the show will be pushed to extremes, behave deliciously badly and have a whole lot of fun along the way. Emma Freeman is the perfect director to take us on the ride, and Netflix have wholeheartedly embraced the scale and ambition of the show.”
A Golden Globe and four-time Emmy nominee, Dockery is best known for starring in the upstairs/downstairs drama Downton Abbey and the associated films. She’s also been seen on shows like Godless, Defending Jacob and Anatomy of a Scandal, with additional film credits including The Gentlemen and Flight Risk. The English actress is repped by United Agents, WME, Anonymous Content, and Johnson Shapiro Slewett & Kole.
O’Reilly is an Irish actress known for her role of Mon Mothma across multiple Star Wars titles, including the recent Disney+ series Andor. Also recently seen starring in Netflix’s early 20th century drama My Brilliant Career, she is repped by RGM Artists, United Agents, Authentic Talent and Literary Management, and Glaser Weil Fink.
This year, Swindell has appeared in the films One Night Only and Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. The New York native’s other credits include the series Prime Target, In Treatment and Trinkets, plus Black Adam, and Paul Schrader’s Master Gardener. Upcoming, they’ll be seen in Neon’s 4 X 4: The Event and A24’s Deep Cuts. They are repped by Gersh, Black Bear, and Myman Greenspan Fox.
De Leon is repped by Gersh, Fusion and Jackoway Austen Tyerman.

Is Netflix’s (NFLX) Free Cash Flow Keeping Pace With Its Reported Earnings?
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 4:22 PM PDT 4 min read
Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) was trading at around $67 on October 5, down 42.35% over twelve months and close to its 52-week low of $65.08. The company reported net income of $13.65 billion over the past twelve months and free cash flow of $11.15 billion.
Cash arriving behind reported profit is the ordinary shape for a company still building, and it is worth understanding before the share price is.
READ ALSO: Amazon (AMZN) and Apple (AAPL) Must Face a UK Class Action Over Marketplace Sales
Is Netflix's (NFLX) Free Cash Flow Keeping Pace With Its Reported Earnings?
The Cash Sits Behind the Profit Because of How Content Is Counted:
The reason sits in how content is counted. Netflix pays for a series up front and then writes the cost off across the years people watch it. The money leaves in one period and the charge against profit lands over several.
That creates a specific signal. When spending on new content runs above the amortization of content already owned, cash falls behind reported profit, because the write-off is still catching up with the paying. Which is exactly the shape of these numbers. On this evidence, the library is being rebuilt rather than harvested.
The underlying business is not the problem. Operating margin is 33.38% and return on equity is 49.54%, on revenue growing 13.40%.
DON'T MISS: What is eBay's (EBAY) Economic Moat, and is it Widening or Narrowing?
Why the Shares Fell Anyway:
A company generating $11.15 billion of free cash flow has lost 42.35% in a year, so the market is pricing something the cash statement does not show. Start with the growth rates. Revenue grew 13.40%, and earnings grew 8.80%.
Profit rising more slowly than sales says a subscriber business has stopped getting cheaper to run, and for a stock valued on compounding that is the end of the easy part. Now put that beside the cash. Rebuilding a library costs money today and defends subscribers tomorrow, so the spending is the reason the cash gap exists at all.
So the cash gap and the weak share price are not describing the same thing. One is the cost of staying competitive, the other is a judgment on what that spending will buy.
Nothing forces the issue. Debt of $16.65 billion against $9.13 billion of cash is comfortable, and Netflix pays no dividend, so an investor earns nothing while waiting. Earnings growing more slowly than sales is the signal that matters here. Ten stocks positioned for high returns in 2026 are named here.
The Valuation Case:
Sustainability depends on content spending, the one lever management fully controls and the one that trades cash today against subscribers tomorrow. On price, the fall has done a great deal of work, taking the trailing multiple to 22.44 times from 51.08 times a year ago.
Enterprise value to EBITDA of 8.64 is the figure that stands out. For a business earning a 33.38% operating margin, under nine times is what the market pays for companies it expects to be smaller.
Price-to-book of 9.85 is the one measure still carrying a premium. A content library is a decade-long asset or a wasting one depending on what gets spent on it, and we looked at 15 stocks built for the next decade in this list.
Conclusion:
Cash flow is running behind earnings, at $11.15 billion against $13.65 billion, and the reason is that Netflix is paying for new content faster than it writes off the old. At 8.64 times enterprise value to EBITDA on a 33.38% operating margin, the price asks very little. However, earnings grew 8.80% against 13.40% revenue growth, and the spending is not yet buying faster profit. The number to watch is content spending, because it decides whether this gap becomes a catalog or just a cost.
Market Sentiment:
Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) was held by 121 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $9.95 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is down from 144 hedge fund holders with a cumulative investment value of around $11.18 billion in the previous quarter.
